text.en: Meena saw a green fuzz on stale bread. "Tiny living things grew there," her teacher said.

Microorganisms are living things that are usually too small to see unaided. Microbiology also studies noncellular entities such as viruses and prions. Microbiology covers bacteria and many microscopic fungi, protists and algae. It also studies viruses and prions, which do not have cellular organisation. Many fungi grow as threads called hyphae. A network of hyphae is a mycelium. Yeasts are single-celled fungi. Some fungi obtain material from living hosts as parasites. Others, called saprotrophs, obtain nutrients from dead or decaying organic matter.
Microbes are useful. Biofertilisers enrich the soil, microbes are used in industries such as making curd and bread, and in medicine such as antibiotics. Some microbes can cause disease, while many do not. The word pathogen refers to an agent capable of causing disease. The incubation period is the time from infection to the first symptoms, when symptoms develop.
Airborne diseases spread through the air, waterborne through unclean water, and vector-borne diseases such as malaria, dengue, chikungunya and filaria through mosquitoes. AIDS and hepatitis-B are among the diseases spread by other routes. Immunisation with vaccines gives protection.

A microscope can let us study objects too small for our eyes to resolve. A single dot in a sketch may stand for a cell with many components.

board.text: A diagram represents structures we cannot see unaided

text.en: Bacteria are usually single cells. A bacterial cell has genetic material but no membrane-bound nucleus. Study these features in a diagram.

board.text: Bacterium: a cell without a membrane-bound nucleus

text.en: Some bacterial cells look round, rod-shaped or curved under a microscope. Shape is one clue. Many different kinds of bacteria can share a similar outline.
A virus particle has genetic material inside a protein coat. Some also have an outer envelope. The drawn particle does not have the structures of a complete cell.

board.text: Virus: genetic material and a coat

text.en: A prion is an abnormally folded protein associated with particular diseases. A protein alone is not a cell, and a prion is different from a bacterium or virus.
One yeast cell contains a nucleus. Many moulds look different because they form networks of threads. Yeasts and moulds belong to the fungi.

board.text: Yeast and mould are both fungi

text.en: In a mould drawing, a single thread is a hypha. Many threads together form a mycelium. A stalk or spore structure is only one part of the drawing.

board.text: Hypha: one thread · mycelium: many threads

text.en: Some protists are single-celled organisms with a nucleus. Amoeba is one example taught in school. Microscopic algae can also live in water and some carry out photosynthesis.
A comparison with a bacterium helps show what the nucleus does as a structural clue. Microscopic size does not tell us whether a cell has a nucleus.

board.text: Size alone does not identify a group

text.en: Decomposers help recycle material from dead plants and animals. They can return nutrients to the surroundings. Many fungi and bacteria take part in this process.
Some soil microorganisms live in close association with roots. Their roles can affect how certain nutrients become available to plants.

board.text: Soil organisms can affect nutrient availability

text.en: Some food industries use microbial activity. Bread and curd are familiar products. The examples show that differing kinds of microbes can cause different changes.

board.text: Food production can use microbial activity

text.en: Some substances discovered in microorganisms have been developed into antibiotics. Antibiotics act against susceptible bacteria. Viruses have different structures and are not the target of antibiotics.

board.text: Antibiotics and viruses involve different targets

text.en: Microbes also contribute to food breakdown and other changes people can observe. Seeing one change in a material does not by itself show which organism caused it.

board.text: A visible change is a clue rather than an identification

text.en: The word infection refers to an infectious agent becoming established in a host. Some infections cause symptoms and some do not. Compare these ideas with the term disease.

board.text: Infection and symptoms describe different observations

text.en: In a health timeline, exposure, infection and symptoms are separate labels. The incubation period is measured from infection to first symptoms. Its length can vary.
People working in public health classify illnesses by patterns. Endemic describes an expected presence in a place or population. An epidemic is more cases than expected in a particular setting.

board.text: Population patterns compare observed and expected cases

text.en: A vector is a living carrier involved in transmission. A textbook example is a mosquito carrying a disease-causing agent. The carrier and the agent are different organisms.
Transmission categories can include spread through air, contaminated water or a vector. The route depends on the agent. Prevention needs to address the relevant route.

board.text: Route names describe how transmission can occur

text.en: Vaccination helps the immune system recognise a particular target. The protection is directed at the disease or agent involved. Study vaccine roles separately from antibiotic roles.
Protection can also involve public measures such as safe water and clean handling of food. Different measures address different sources of risk.
When a claim says all microbes are harmful, compare the evidence from decomposition and food production. The word microbe covers many kinds of organisms with different effects.

board.text: Some cause illness; others are useful or have little effect on us

problem.en: One diagram shows a bacterial cell and another shows a virus particle. Which structural clues help distinguish them?

text.en: Find the drawing with a cell boundary and internal cell contents.

why.en: The picture shows a virus particle rather than a complete cell.

prompt.en: A friend says All microbes cause disease. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: They make curd, biofertilisers and medicines.

points.en: Microbiology studies tiny cellular organisms and noncellular agents such as viruses.
Vaccines can prepare the immune system for a particular target.
